script.opening: "It’s just my sleeping tablets, doctor. The chemist said I had to see you. And between you and me — they’re not working like they used to. My friend Brenda gets the blue ones, temazepam — could I try those?"

facts.text: Fell last Tuesday at 3am on the way to the toilet. "My legs just weren’t under me." Bruised hip and shoulder; X-ray clear. First fall, but she’s felt "woozy" at night for months.
Takes the tablet at 9.30pm, asleep by 10.30, wakes at 2–3am most nights and lies awake. Naps in the chair most afternoons. Believes without the tablet she would "never sleep again".
Has crept up: occasionally takes "a half extra" when wakeful at 3am — which is why the repeat is early. Embarrassed when this surfaces.
Started the month Arthur died, 12 years ago. "Dr Pearson said it would just be for a few weeks." Nobody has ever reviewed it since.
Evenings are the hard part — "the house gets very quiet at nine o’clock". Not depressed by her account: enjoys church, bowls club Tuesdays, the grandchildren. But dreads the nights.
Sherry "most evenings, just the one". Tea all day including with supper. Watches TV in bed when wakeful.

ice.ideas: The tablets have "stopped working" and a stronger one would fix the waking.
ice.concerns: Terrified of nights without a tablet — "I lie there thinking about Arthur". Quietly shaken by the fall but hasn’t connected it to the zopiclone.
ice.expectations: A repeat today, ideally something stronger. Definitely not "being told off".

cues: "The house gets very quiet at nine o’clock" — the loneliness behind the insomnia.
Looks down and goes quiet when the early repeat is mentioned — shame, not deceit.
"I don’t want to end up doddery like my sister" — fear of falling and of decline, the lever for change.

checkpoints.text: Connects the fall to the zopiclone explicitly (hypnotics are a recognised cause of night-time falls in older people, and NICE NG249 puts medication review at the centre of a falls assessment) and checks orthostatic symptoms / reviews amlodipine timing
Recognises tolerance and dependence after 12 years — names them without blame, and does NOT escalate to temazepam or prescribe "something stronger"

Negotiates a gradual taper (e.g. 3.75 mg on alternate nights, then nightly, with further steps agreed every few weeks — expect months) — never abrupt cessation; explicitly warns against stopping suddenly
Offers what replaces the tablet: sleep-restriction/CBT-I principles, caffeine and sherry timing, no TV in bed, afternoon nap capped
Hears the grief and the quiet house — the insomnia is partly loneliness, and says so kindly
Handles the early-repeat shame gently — curiosity, not accusation
Uses HER motivation (fear of falls, "doddery like my sister") as the engine of the taper, not the GP’s agenda
Safety-nets the taper: rebound insomnia for a fortnight is expected and temporary; falls advice (light on, sit on bed edge first); books named follow-up in 2–4 weeks

worked.txt: "I’m not going to take your tablet away today. But the fall changes things — these tablets and 3am legs are a known bad mix, and I’d be a poor doctor if I just made them stronger."
"After twelve years the tablet isn’t really giving you sleep any more — your body has learned it. What it IS still doing is the wooziness that put you on the floor last week."
"Lots of people take an extra half at 3am — you’re not in trouble. It tells me the tablet has stopped doing its job, not that you’ve done something wrong."
"Tell me about nine o’clock. What would a good evening look like, if the house weren’t so quiet?"
"You said it yourself — you don’t want to end up like your sister. The single best fall-prevention step you can take is the one we’ve just talked about."

"The first two weeks of cutting down, sleep gets briefly worse before it resets — that’s the tablet leaving, not your insomnia returning. If you’re struggling, ring me rather than ride it out alone. I want to see you in three weeks either way."

f.learning: Z-drugs and benzodiazepines raise the risk of falls and fractures in older people, and tolerance makes long-term use ineffective for sleep. The exam skill is deprescribing as a negotiation: validate the fear, harness the patient’s own motivation, taper slowly (never stop abruptly), and replace the tablet with something — CBT-I principles and attention to the loneliness driving the 3am waking. Escalating to temazepam is the station’s trapdoor.

knowledge.guideline: NICE TA77 (2004) — hypnotics for insomnia · NICE NG249 (2025) — falls · NICE HTG624 (Sleepio, formerly MTG70)
knowledge.summary: Twelve years of nightly zopiclone means tolerance and dependence, not insomnia needing a stronger drug. After a night-time fall, the hypnotic is part of the falls review: taper it slowly by agreement, never stop it abruptly, never escalate to temazepam, and replace it with CBT-I principles.

points.t: NICE TA77: hypnotics only after non-drug measures have been considered, and only short term. There is no compelling evidence to separate z-drugs from short-acting benzodiazepines, so switching to temazepam offers nothing but a different name and a stricter controlled-drug status.

Asleep at 10.30pm, awake at 2–3am, afternoon naps, an extra half tablet at 3am and an early repeat: tolerance and dependence, with fragmented sleep driven by napping, evening alcohol, tea and TV in bed — and grief. More drug cannot fix this pattern.

points.h: The fall is the red flag
points.t: NICE NG249: an older person who has fallen needs a multifactorial falls risk assessment, including a medication review. Here that means the hypnotic plus sherry, amlodipine and postural symptoms (lying and standing BP), vision, footwear, night-time route to the toilet and bone health.

Withdraw gradually after long-term use; abrupt withdrawal risks rebound insomnia, anxiety and withdrawal symptoms. A natural first step is 3.75 mg — the BNF starting dose for older people — on alternate nights, then nightly, with further steps agreed with her every few weeks. Expect the process to take months.

CBT-I is first-line for chronic insomnia (BAP consensus 2019): fixed rising time, bed only for sleep, get up if awake and frustrated, short or no daytime nap, caffeine only in the morning. Digital CBT-I (Sleepio) is recommended in NICE HTG624 (formerly MTG70). Screen mood (NICE NG222) and name the loneliness behind the 3am waking.

Sherry potentiates zopiclone’s sedation and worsens night-time unsteadiness — move it earlier or stop it on tablet nights. Zopiclone is a Schedule 4 (Part 1) and temazepam a Schedule 3 controlled drug (Home Office Circular 008/2014).

dg.d: Open question first; let her voice the repeat and the temazepam request before steering; explored a typical night in her words.
Lives alone, widowed 12 years, daughter nearby, church and bowls; evening routine, sherry, tea, TV in bed.
Lying and standing BP, falls risk assessment, medication review including amlodipine, bone-health assessment, mood screen.
Tolerance and dependence vs depression vs sleep-behaviour problems; hypnotic- and alcohol-related fall vs syncope or postural hypotension.
Asked about blackouts, palpitations, head injury and injuries from the fall; checked for low mood and hopelessness.
Long-term hypnotic dependence with tolerance, contributing to a night-time fall; insomnia sustained by napping, alcohol and grief.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: No escalation to temazepam; gradual agreed taper starting at 3.75 mg (never abrupt); CBT-I principles and digital CBT-I; sherry moved earlier.
Falls review, postural BP and amlodipine timing, bone health; loneliness and bereavement support.
Rebound insomnia expected and temporary; do not take extra; night-time falls advice; named review in 2–4 weeks with a limited supply.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “the house gets quiet at nine”, the silence over the early repeat, and “doddery like my sister”.
Idea: the tablet has stopped working and a stronger one will help; concern: nights without a tablet, grief, the fall; expectation: a repeat and no telling-off.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Terrified of nights without a tablet — "I lie there thinking about Arthur". Quietly shaken by the fall but hasn’t connected it to the zopiclone — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Hardcastle, I’m Dr Shah. Thank you for joining — and I gather your daughter helped set up the video. Before we get to the prescription, tell me how things have been for you.
model.why: Opens with the patient, not the repeat request

model.text: It’s just my sleeping tablets, doctor. The chemist said I had to see you. And between you and me — they’re not working like they used to. My friend Brenda gets the blue ones, temazepam. Could I try those?

Thank you for being so straight with me — I’ll be straight with you too. I’d like to hear how your nights actually go, and I also saw a note about a fall last week, so I’d like to cover both and then decide together what to do about the tablets. Is that alright?
model.why: Agenda that holds her request and the fall together

model.text: Oh, the fall. Yes, that was silly of me. Alright.
Walk me through a typical night, from the evening onwards.
model.why: Open question before narrowing

model.text: Tablet at half past nine, asleep by half ten. Then I’m wide awake at two or three, just lying there. I do nod off in the chair most afternoons, I’m afraid.
And the fall — what happened?

Tuesday, three in the morning, going to the loo. My legs just weren’t under me. Bruised my hip and shoulder; they X-rayed it and nothing was broken. I’ve felt a bit woozy at night for months, to be honest.
Did you black out at all, or feel your heart racing, or feel light-headed as you stood up? And had you taken anything extra that night?
model.why: Screens syncope, postural symptoms and usage in one sweep

model.text: No blackout. Light-headed getting up, maybe. (Pause.) I might have had a half extra. I do sometimes, when I can’t get back off. That’s why I’m early, isn’t it. I’m sorry.
Please don’t apologise — lots of people do exactly that. It tells me the tablet has stopped doing its job, not that you’ve done anything wrong.
model.why: Meets the shame with curiosity, not accusation

model.text: Well. That’s a relief.
Do you have a drink in the evening, or tea later on? And what do you do when you’re lying awake?
model.why: Alcohol, caffeine and sleep behaviours that feed the waking

model.text: A sherry most evenings, just the one. Tea all day, one with supper. I put the telly on in bed when I can’t sleep.
And how’s your mood — are you still enjoying things?
model.why: Screens for depression as a driver of early waking

model.text: Oh yes. Church, bowls on Tuesdays, the grandchildren. It’s just… the house gets very quiet at nine o’clock.
The house gets very quiet at nine. Tell me about that.
model.why: Picks up the loneliness cue word for word

model.text: Arthur and I always had our cocoa at nine. He died twelve years ago — that’s when Dr Pearson gave me the tablets. Just for a few weeks, he said. When I wake at three, I lie there thinking about him.
Twelve years, and the nights are still the hardest part. Thank you for telling me about Arthur. What were you hoping I’d do for you today?
model.why: Acknowledges the grief, then elicits expectations

model.text: Just the repeat, really. Something stronger if you could. And I didn’t want to be told off.
Nobody’s telling you off. Can I ask — did the fall worry you?
model.why: Opens her own concern about the fall

model.text: It did, if I’m honest. I don’t want to end up doddery like my sister. She had a fall and never went back home.

That matters, and I’d like to build on it. Here’s what I think is going on. After twelve years your body has got used to the tablet — it isn’t really giving you sleep any more, which is why you wake at three. What it is still doing is making your legs unsteady in the night, and the sherry adds to that. Sleeping tablets are a well-known cause of night-time falls in people your age.
model.why: Names tolerance and links the fall to the hypnotic

model.text: I never thought of the tablet. I thought it was just my age.

That’s a very fair thing to think. It’s also why I won’t prescribe temazepam or anything stronger: it works in the same way, it wouldn’t fix the waking, and it would make another fall more likely. After last week, I’d be letting you down if I did.
model.why: Declines escalation with a reason tied to her

model.text: So you’re stopping them? I’ll never sleep again.

No — I’m not taking your tablet away today. After this long, stopping suddenly isn’t safe; it makes sleep much worse and can leave you shaky and anxious. What I’d suggest is coming down slowly, at a pace you’re comfortable with, while we put something else in place for the nights.
model.why: Explicitly warns against abrupt cessation; offers a taper

model.text: What would that look like?

The first step would be half a tablet — which is actually the usual starting dose for someone your age — on alternate nights, then every night. We only move on when you feel ready, and I’ll check in every few weeks. It may take a few months, and that’s fine.
model.why: Concrete, gradual, patient-paced taper

model.text: Every other night. I could try that.

Alongside it, some changes that do more for the 3am waking than the tablet can: the same getting-up time every day, no telly in bed, keep any afternoon nap short, and decaf tea after lunch. There’s also a well-tested sleep programme you can do on a tablet or computer. Could your daughter help you set that up?
model.why: Replaces the tablet with CBT-I principles

model.text: She could. I’d give it a go.
And the sherry — could it move to teatime, well away from the tablet?
model.why: Negotiates one change rather than banning it

model.text: I could have it with my tea at six instead.

Perfect. And nine o’clock — would it help to have something that’s yours in that hour? A phone call with your daughter, perhaps, and I can give you details of a bereavement charity that offers someone to talk to. The nights have been lonely for a long time.
model.why: Addresses the loneliness driving the insomnia

model.text: Ringing my daughter at nine… she’d like that, actually.

I’d also like the nurse to check your blood pressure lying and standing, look at your blood-pressure tablet, and do a proper falls check including your bones. You said you don’t want to end up like your sister — this plan is the best thing you can do about exactly that.
model.why: Falls review, and uses her own motivation as the lever

model.text: Well, when you put it like that.

Two things to expect. When you first cut down, sleep may get worse for a week or two — that’s the tablet leaving, not your insomnia coming back, and it settles. Please don’t take extra to cover it; ring me instead. And at night: a lamp on, sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing, and keep the way to the loo clear.
model.why: Safety-nets rebound insomnia and gives falls advice

model.text: Lamp on, sit first. Yes.

If you fall again or feel faint, ring us that day. I’ll issue enough tablets to take you to our next appointment on the plan we’ve agreed, and I’ll see you in three weeks. So I know I’ve explained it well — what will you tell your daughter we’ve agreed?
model.why: Named follow-up, controlled supply, teach-back

model.text: Half a tablet every other night to start, no telly in bed, sherry at teatime, lamp on, ring her at nine, and back to you in three weeks.
That’s it exactly. Is there anything else you wanted to ask?
model.why: Shares the floor before closing

model.text: No, that’s plenty. Thank you, doctor — I thought you’d be cross.

social.t: Widowed 12 years and living alone; the evening routine she shared with Arthur is the hardest hour. Loneliness drives the 3am waking as much as the tablet does — name it kindly and offer something for that hour.
A nearby daughter who can help with digital CBT-I and a nightly phone call; her sister’s fall and move into care is her fear and her motivation to change.

legal.t: Zopiclone is a Class C, Schedule 4 (Part 1) controlled drug and temazepam a Schedule 3 controlled drug (Home Office Circular 008/2014). Limit supplies during a taper and record the plan.
If she drives: zopiclone can impair next-day driving, and it is an offence to drive while impaired by any drug, prescribed or not. Advise not to drive if she feels drowsy.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): repeat prescriptions must be reviewed. Twelve years without review is a system failure — handle it without blaming her or a colleague.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): the taper is her choice to make with clear information about benefits and risks. Document the agreed steps, the falls discussion and the review date.

community.t: Community falls-prevention service and strength-and-balance classes; Cruse Bereavement Support; Age UK for befriending; digital CBT-I (Sleepio, NICE HTG624, formerly MTG70).

redFlags: The night-time fall: blackout, palpitations or chest pain (possible syncope), head injury, new confusion
Postural light-headedness on standing — check lying and standing BP and amlodipine timing
Mood: early waking with hopelessness or loss of enjoyment would point to depression
psychosocial: Widowed 12 years, lives alone; evenings are the hard part
Sherry most evenings with the tablet, tea all day, TV in bed, afternoon naps
What independence means to her — her sister’s fall and move into care
ice: Idea: “the tablets have stopped working; a stronger one would fix the waking”
Concern: nights without a tablet — “I lie there thinking about Arthur”; quietly shaken by the fall
Expectation: a repeat today, ideally stronger — and not to be told off

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest and kind: “After twelve years your body has got used to the tablet, so it isn’t really giving you sleep any more — but it is still making you unsteady at night, and that is very likely part of why you fell.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s like a key that’s been used so long the lock no longer turns — it doesn’t open the door to sleep any more, but it still makes the floor feel slippery at three in the morning.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you don’t want to end up like your sister. Coming off this tablet slowly is one of the most useful things you can do to stay steady and stay in your own home.”
management.psychosocial: Give nine o’clock a new shape — a nightly call with her daughter, bereavement support if she wants it — and agree one or two sleep changes she chooses rather than a list of rules.
sharedPlan: No temazepam or stronger hypnotic; gradual taper starting at 3.75 mg on alternate nights, then nightly, reviewed every few weeks
CBT-I principles (fixed rising time, no TV in bed, short or no nap, decaf after lunch) and digital CBT-I
Falls review: lying and standing BP, amlodipine review, bone health; sherry moved to teatime
safetyNet: Sleep may worsen for a week or two after each step — expected and temporary; do not take extra, ring instead
Lamp on, sit before standing; ring the same day after any further fall or faint; review in three weeks

pitfalls.intro: This station is not failed for lack of pharmacology — it is failed by handing over the repeat, by escalating to a stronger hypnotic, or by stopping the tablet with a lecture. The patterns below are the common failing routes, and each is fixable.

items.fail: Switching to temazepam because “the zopiclone has stopped working”.
items.why: NICE TA77 finds no meaningful difference between z-drugs and short-acting benzodiazepines; escalating a hypnotic a week after a night-time fall is unsafe management.
items.fix: Decline with a reason tied to her: “It works the same way, it wouldn’t fix the waking, and it would make another fall more likely.”

items.fail: Stopping the zopiclone today because of the fall.
items.why: Abrupt withdrawal after 12 years risks severe rebound insomnia and withdrawal symptoms — and she will simply not engage again.
items.fix: Say out loud that stopping suddenly is not safe, then agree a gradual taper starting at 3.75 mg on alternate nights, reviewed every few weeks.

items.fail: Treating the fall and the prescription as two separate problems.
items.why: The link between the hypnotic, the sherry and the 3am fall is the clinical heart of the case; missing it means no falls review (NICE NG249) and no reason for her to change.
items.fix: Ask about the fall early, screen for syncope and postural symptoms, and name the connection plainly.

items.fail: Asking “why are you two weeks early?” in a tone that sounds like an audit.
items.why: She goes quiet out of shame, not deceit; an accusing question loses the usage history and her trust.
items.fix: Normalise first — “lots of people take an extra half at 3am” — and she will tell you the rest.

items.fail: Missing “the house gets very quiet at nine o’clock”.
items.why: The grief and loneliness are the engine of the insomnia; a plan that ignores them feels like having a comfort taken away.
items.fix: Reflect the cue back, let Arthur be spoken about, and offer something for that hour — a call, bereavement support, a routine.

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll cut it down and see how you get on”, with no warning about rebound insomnia and no review date.
items.why: Without warning, the first bad night convinces her the plan has failed and she tops up; without follow-up the taper stalls.
items.fix: Warn that sleep worsens briefly after each step, ask her to ring rather than take extra, give falls advice for the night and book a named review in three weeks.

SCA_MODELS.text: A sherry most evenings, just the one. Tea all day, one with supper. I put the telly on in bed when I can’t sleep.
And how’s your mood — are you still enjoying things?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for depression as a driver of early waking

SCA_MODELS.text: Oh yes. Church, bowls on Tuesdays, the grandchildren. It’s just… the house gets very quiet at nine o’clock.
The house gets very quiet at nine. Tell me about that.
SCA_MODELS.why: Picks up the loneliness cue word for word

SCA_MODELS.text: Arthur and I always had our cocoa at nine. He died twelve years ago — that’s when Dr Pearson gave me the tablets. Just for a few weeks, he said. When I wake at three, I lie there thinking about him.
Twelve years, and the nights are still the hardest part. Thank you for telling me about Arthur. What were you hoping I’d do for you today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Acknowledges the grief, then elicits expectations

SCA_MODELS.text: Just the repeat, really. Something stronger if you could. And I didn’t want to be told off.
Nobody’s telling you off. Can I ask — did the fall worry you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Opens her own concern about the fall

SCA_MODELS.text: It did, if I’m honest. I don’t want to end up doddery like my sister. She had a fall and never went back home.

That matters, and I’d like to build on it. Here’s what I think is going on. After twelve years your body has got used to the tablet — it isn’t really giving you sleep any more, which is why you wake at three. What it is still doing is making your legs unsteady in the night, and the sherry adds to that. Sleeping tablets are a well-known cause of night-time falls in people your age.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names tolerance and links the fall to the hypnotic

SCA_MODELS.text: I never thought of the tablet. I thought it was just my age.

That’s a very fair thing to think. It’s also why I won’t prescribe temazepam or anything stronger: it works in the same way, it wouldn’t fix the waking, and it would make another fall more likely. After last week, I’d be letting you down if I did.
SCA_MODELS.why: Declines escalation with a reason tied to her

SCA_MODELS.text: So you’re stopping them? I’ll never sleep again.

No — I’m not taking your tablet away today. After this long, stopping suddenly isn’t safe; it makes sleep much worse and can leave you shaky and anxious. What I’d suggest is coming down slowly, at a pace you’re comfortable with, while we put something else in place for the nights.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explicitly warns against abrupt cessation; offers a taper

SCA_MODELS.text: What would that look like?

The first step would be half a tablet — which is actually the usual starting dose for someone your age — on alternate nights, then every night. We only move on when you feel ready, and I’ll check in every few weeks. It may take a few months, and that’s fine.
SCA_MODELS.why: Concrete, gradual, patient-paced taper

SCA_MODELS.text: Every other night. I could try that.

Alongside it, some changes that do more for the 3am waking than the tablet can: the same getting-up time every day, no telly in bed, keep any afternoon nap short, and decaf tea after lunch. There’s also a well-tested sleep programme you can do on a tablet or computer. Could your daughter help you set that up?
SCA_MODELS.why: Replaces the tablet with CBT-I principles

SCA_MODELS.text: She could. I’d give it a go.
And the sherry — could it move to teatime, well away from the tablet?
SCA_MODELS.why: Negotiates one change rather than banning it

SCA_MODELS.text: I could have it with my tea at six instead.

Perfect. And nine o’clock — would it help to have something that’s yours in that hour? A phone call with your daughter, perhaps, and I can give you details of a bereavement charity that offers someone to talk to. The nights have been lonely for a long time.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the loneliness driving the insomnia

SCA_MODELS.text: Ringing my daughter at nine… she’d like that, actually.

I’d also like the nurse to check your blood pressure lying and standing, look at your blood-pressure tablet, and do a proper falls check including your bones. You said you don’t want to end up like your sister — this plan is the best thing you can do about exactly that.
SCA_MODELS.why: Falls review, and uses her own motivation as the lever

SCA_MODELS.text: Well, when you put it like that.

Two things to expect. When you first cut down, sleep may get worse for a week or two — that’s the tablet leaving, not your insomnia coming back, and it settles. Please don’t take extra to cover it; ring me instead. And at night: a lamp on, sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing, and keep the way to the loo clear.
SCA_MODELS.why: Safety-nets rebound insomnia and gives falls advice

SCA_MODELS.text: Lamp on, sit first. Yes.

If you fall again or feel faint, ring us that day. I’ll issue enough tablets to take you to our next appointment on the plan we’ve agreed, and I’ll see you in three weeks. So I know I’ve explained it well — what will you tell your daughter we’ve agreed?
SCA_MODELS.why: Named follow-up, controlled supply, teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Half a tablet every other night to start, no telly in bed, sherry at teatime, lamp on, ring her at nine, and back to you in three weeks.
That’s it exactly. Is there anything else you wanted to ask?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares the floor before closing

SCA_MODELS.text: No, that’s plenty. Thank you, doctor — I thought you’d be cross.

SCA_STEM.name: Jean Hardcastle
pmh: Fall at home last week — bruised hip and shoulder, X-ray normal (urgent treatment centre)
meds: Zopiclone 7.5 mg at night (on repeat for 12 years, started after bereavement)
SCA_STEM.recent: Seen in the urgent treatment centre last week after a fall at 3am on the way to the toilet — no fracture. Zopiclone repeat requested two weeks early; flagged by reception. No medication review recorded for the zopiclone. Widowed 12 years; lives alone, daughter nearby.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation (set up by her daughter) to request her zopiclone repeat.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE TA77 (2004) — hypnotics for insomnia · NICE NG249 (2025) — falls · NICE HTG624 (Sleepio, formerly MTG70)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Twelve years of nightly zopiclone means tolerance and dependence, not insomnia needing a stronger drug. After a night-time fall, the hypnotic is part of the falls review: taper it slowly by agreement, never stop it abruptly, never escalate to temazepam, and replace it with CBT-I principles.

points.t: NICE TA77: hypnotics only after non-drug measures have been considered, and only short term. There is no compelling evidence to separate z-drugs from short-acting benzodiazepines, so switching to temazepam offers nothing but a different name and a stricter controlled-drug status.

Asleep at 10.30pm, awake at 2–3am, afternoon naps, an extra half tablet at 3am and an early repeat: tolerance and dependence, with fragmented sleep driven by napping, evening alcohol, tea and TV in bed — and grief. More drug cannot fix this pattern.

points.h: The fall is the red flag
points.t: NICE NG249: an older person who has fallen needs a multifactorial falls risk assessment, including a medication review. Here that means the hypnotic plus sherry, amlodipine and postural symptoms (lying and standing BP), vision, footwear, night-time route to the toilet and bone health.

Withdraw gradually after long-term use; abrupt withdrawal risks rebound insomnia, anxiety and withdrawal symptoms. A natural first step is 3.75 mg — the BNF starting dose for older people — on alternate nights, then nightly, with further steps agreed with her every few weeks. Expect the process to take months.

CBT-I is first-line for chronic insomnia (BAP consensus 2019): fixed rising time, bed only for sleep, get up if awake and frustrated, short or no daytime nap, caffeine only in the morning. Digital CBT-I (Sleepio) is recommended in NICE HTG624 (formerly MTG70). Screen mood (NICE NG222) and name the loneliness behind the 3am waking.

Sherry potentiates zopiclone’s sedation and worsens night-time unsteadiness — move it earlier or stop it on tablet nights. Zopiclone is a Schedule 4 (Part 1) and temazepam a Schedule 3 controlled drug (Home Office Circular 008/2014).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; let her voice the repeat and the temazepam request before steering; explored a typical night in her words.
Lives alone, widowed 12 years, daughter nearby, church and bowls; evening routine, sherry, tea, TV in bed.
Picked up “the house gets quiet at nine”, the silence over the early repeat, and “doddery like my sister”.
Idea: the tablet has stopped working and a stronger one will help; concern: nights without a tablet, grief, the fall; expectation: a repeat and no telling-off.
Lying and standing BP, falls risk assessment, medication review including amlodipine, bone-health assessment, mood screen.
Tolerance and dependence vs depression vs sleep-behaviour problems; hypnotic- and alcohol-related fall vs syncope or postural hypotension.
Asked about blackouts, palpitations, head injury and injuries from the fall; checked for low mood and hopelessness.
Long-term hypnotic dependence with tolerance, contributing to a night-time fall; insomnia sustained by napping, alcohol and grief.
No escalation to temazepam; gradual agreed taper starting at 3.75 mg (never abrupt); CBT-I principles and digital CBT-I; sherry moved earlier.
Falls review, postural BP and amlodipine timing, bone health; loneliness and bereavement support.
Rebound insomnia expected and temporary; do not take extra; night-time falls advice; named review in 2–4 weeks with a limited supply.

social.t: Widowed 12 years and living alone; the evening routine she shared with Arthur is the hardest hour. Loneliness drives the 3am waking as much as the tablet does — name it kindly and offer something for that hour.
A nearby daughter who can help with digital CBT-I and a nightly phone call; her sister’s fall and move into care is her fear and her motivation to change.

legal.t: Zopiclone is a Class C, Schedule 4 (Part 1) controlled drug and temazepam a Schedule 3 controlled drug (Home Office Circular 008/2014). Limit supplies during a taper and record the plan.
If she drives: zopiclone can impair next-day driving, and it is an offence to drive while impaired by any drug, prescribed or not. Advise not to drive if she feels drowsy.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): repeat prescriptions must be reviewed. Twelve years without review is a system failure — handle it without blaming her or a colleague.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): the taper is her choice to make with clear information about benefits and risks. Document the agreed steps, the falls discussion and the review date.

community.t: Community falls-prevention service and strength-and-balance classes; Cruse Bereavement Support; Age UK for befriending; digital CBT-I (Sleepio, NICE HTG624, formerly MTG70).

redFlags: The night-time fall: blackout, palpitations or chest pain (possible syncope), head injury, new confusion
Postural light-headedness on standing — check lying and standing BP and amlodipine timing
Mood: early waking with hopelessness or loss of enjoyment would point to depression
psychosocial: Widowed 12 years, lives alone; evenings are the hard part
Sherry most evenings with the tablet, tea all day, TV in bed, afternoon naps
What independence means to her — her sister’s fall and move into care
ice: Idea: “the tablets have stopped working; a stronger one would fix the waking”
Concern: nights without a tablet — “I lie there thinking about Arthur”; quietly shaken by the fall
Expectation: a repeat today, ideally stronger — and not to be told off

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest and kind: “After twelve years your body has got used to the tablet, so it isn’t really giving you sleep any more — but it is still making you unsteady at night, and that is very likely part of why you fell.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s like a key that’s been used so long the lock no longer turns — it doesn’t open the door to sleep any more, but it still makes the floor feel slippery at three in the morning.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you don’t want to end up like your sister. Coming off this tablet slowly is one of the most useful things you can do to stay steady and stay in your own home.”
management.psychosocial: Give nine o’clock a new shape — a nightly call with her daughter, bereavement support if she wants it — and agree one or two sleep changes she chooses rather than a list of rules.
sharedPlan: No temazepam or stronger hypnotic; gradual taper starting at 3.75 mg on alternate nights, then nightly, reviewed every few weeks
CBT-I principles (fixed rising time, no TV in bed, short or no nap, decaf after lunch) and digital CBT-I
Falls review: lying and standing BP, amlodipine review, bone health; sherry moved to teatime
safetyNet: Sleep may worsen for a week or two after each step — expected and temporary; do not take extra, ring instead
Lamp on, sit before standing; ring the same day after any further fall or faint; review in three weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is not failed for lack of pharmacology — it is failed by handing over the repeat, by escalating to a stronger hypnotic, or by stopping the tablet with a lecture. The patterns below are the common failing routes, and each is fixable.

items.fail: Switching to temazepam because “the zopiclone has stopped working”.
items.why: NICE TA77 finds no meaningful difference between z-drugs and short-acting benzodiazepines; escalating a hypnotic a week after a night-time fall is unsafe management.
items.fix: Decline with a reason tied to her: “It works the same way, it wouldn’t fix the waking, and it would make another fall more likely.”

items.fail: Stopping the zopiclone today because of the fall.
items.why: Abrupt withdrawal after 12 years risks severe rebound insomnia and withdrawal symptoms — and she will simply not engage again.
items.fix: Say out loud that stopping suddenly is not safe, then agree a gradual taper starting at 3.75 mg on alternate nights, reviewed every few weeks.

items.fail: Treating the fall and the prescription as two separate problems.
items.why: The link between the hypnotic, the sherry and the 3am fall is the clinical heart of the case; missing it means no falls review (NICE NG249) and no reason for her to change.
items.fix: Ask about the fall early, screen for syncope and postural symptoms, and name the connection plainly.

items.fail: Asking “why are you two weeks early?” in a tone that sounds like an audit.
items.why: She goes quiet out of shame, not deceit; an accusing question loses the usage history and her trust.
items.fix: Normalise first — “lots of people take an extra half at 3am” — and she will tell you the rest.

items.fail: Missing “the house gets very quiet at nine o’clock”.
items.why: The grief and loneliness are the engine of the insomnia; a plan that ignores them feels like having a comfort taken away.
items.fix: Reflect the cue back, let Arthur be spoken about, and offer something for that hour — a call, bereavement support, a routine.

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll cut it down and see how you get on”, with no warning about rebound insomnia and no review date.
items.why: Without warning, the first bad night convinces her the plan has failed and she tops up; without follow-up the taper stalls.
items.fix: Warn that sleep worsens briefly after each step, ask her to ring rather than take extra, give falls advice for the night and book a named review in three weeks.
